Key Characteristics & Origin: Secretory type (sIgA) is a dimer/trimer with a J-chain and a secretory piece; monomer in serum. Produced by mucosal plasma cells.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Provides mucosal immunity; dimer secretory piece resists digestive enzymes and coats/neutralizes pathogens on mucosal surfaces, preventing epithelial attachment.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Selective IgA Deficiency (causes recurrent sinopulmonary and GI infections); IgA Nephropathy (Berger's disease); Henoch-Schönlein purpura.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum IgA levels (<7 mg/dL defines selective deficiency); immunofluorescence showing IgA mesangial deposits in kidney biopsy.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Most abundant class in serum (~75%); monomeric structure. Secreted in high amounts by plasma cells during the secondary adaptive immune response.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Functions as a primary defender against bacteria, viruses, and toxins via neutralization, opsonization (promoting macrophage phagocytosis via Fc receptor binding), complement activation, and ADCC via NK cells; uniquely crosses the placenta.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Autoimmune hemolytic anemia and Erythroblastosis Fetalis (Type II hypersensitivity); IgG autoantibody deficiencies cause recurrent pyogenic infections.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Quantitative serum IgG levels; immunofluorescence showing IgG deposition; positive Coombs test (for autoimmune hemolytic anemia).

Key Characteristics & Origin: Pentameric structure linked by disulfide bonds and a J-chain in secretions; monomeric on mature B cell surfaces as a B cell receptor (BCR). Earliest antibody produced in a primary immune response.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Exhibits high avidity with 10 antigen-binding sites; exceptionally potent at complement activation (complement fixing) and causing agglutination (clumping) of pathogens.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion reactions (Type II hypersensitivity); participates in Type III immune complex-mediated hypersensitivities; cold agglutinin disease.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Quantitative serum IgM levels; isohemagglutinin titer; direct/indirect agglutination assays.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Monomeric structure; co-expressed with IgM on the surface of mature, naive B lymphocytes. Very low concentration in normal serum (~0.2%).
Primary Function & Mechanism: Functions primarily as a membrane-bound antigen receptor (BCR partner) to assist in B cell activation, maturation, and survival signaling.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Hyper-IgD syndrome (a periodic fever syndrome marked by high IgD levels and recurrent inflammatory episodes); levels vary in chronic inflammatory diseases.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry showing surface IgD+ on mature naive B cells (CD19+ / CD20+ / IgM+ / IgD+); serum IgD levels measured by ELISA or nephelometry.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Lowest concentration in normal serum; monomeric structure with an extra constant domain (CH4). Produced by plasma cells following isotype switching induced by IL-4.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds with extremely high affinity to FcεRI receptors on mast cells and basophils. Cross-linking by allergens triggers immediate cell degranulation, releasing preformed inflammatory mediators.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Mediates Type I hypersensitivity (allergic rhinitis, asthma, hives, systemic anaphylaxis); plays an essential defensive role against helminthic parasite infections.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Elevated total serum IgE levels; allergen-specific IgE testing (RAST/ImmunoCAP); skin prick wheel-and-flare testing.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Highly pure, monospecific antibodies manufactured in vitro. Produced by fusing a specific plasma B cell with an immortal myeloma cell to create a hybridoma.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds with absolute specificity to a single epitope on a target antigen, enabling targeted neutralisation, cell labeling, or receptor blocking.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Used as therapeutics: Rituximab (anti-CD20 for B cell lymphoma and RA), Infliximab (anti-TNF-α for Crohn's and RA), Trastuzumab (anti-HER2 for breast cancer).
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Purity checked via capillary electrophoresis; binding specificity validated via ELISA and Western blot.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Rapid, IgE-mediated systemic or local allergic reaction occurring within minutes of re-exposure to an allergen in a sensitized individual.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Allergen cross-links IgE antibodies pre-bound to high-affinity FcεRI receptors on mast cells/basophils. Degranulation releases histamine (early phase) and stimulates leukotriene synthesis (late phase).
Clinical & Disease Associations: Anaphylactic shock (marked by massive systemic vasodilation, bronchial smooth muscle contraction, and laryngeal edema); allergic asthma; food allergies.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Clinical diagnosis; elevated serum tryptase (marker of mast cell degranulation) measured shortly after the episode; skin prick testing.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Antibody-mediated cytotoxic reaction targeting antigens present on specific cell surfaces or within extracellular matrix tissues.
Primary Function & Mechanism: IgG or IgM antibodies bind directly to target cells, triggering classical complement activation (MAC lysis), opsonization for phagocytosis, or NK cell-mediated ADCC.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Mismatched ABO blood transfusion reactions, Erythroblastosis Fetalis (hemolytic disease of the newborn), Myasthenia Gravis, Autoimmune Hemolytic Anemia, Goodpasture's syndrome.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Direct and Indirect Coombs tests; detection of tissue-specific autoantibodies (e.g., anti-AChR); immunofluorescence biopsy showing linear deposition.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Immune complex-mediated inflammatory reaction caused by the deposition of circulating, medium-sized antigen-antibody complexes in filters and tissues.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Circulating complexes deposit in blood vessels, joint synovium, or glomeruli, where they activate complement and recruit neutrophils that release destructive lysosomal enzymes.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE), Rheumatoid Arthritis (RA), Serum Sickness, Arthus reaction, Post-streptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Decreased serum C3 and C4 complement levels; presence of circulating immune complexes; tissue biopsies showing granular (lumpy) immune deposits under immunofluorescence.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Delayed-type, cell-mediated (antibody-independent) inflammatory reaction; peaks 48-72 hours after physical skin contact with an active hapten.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Haptens (e.g., poison ivy pentadecacatechol, nickel, leather chemicals) bind self-proteins, becoming immunogenic. Dendritic cells present them to Th1 cells, which secrete IFN-γ to recruit and activate highly destructive macrophages.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Pruritic, vesicular, erythematous skin lesions localized to the area of contact; localized tissue injury and swelling; Tuberculin skin test; graft rejection.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Patch testing (application of suspected allergens to the skin for 48 hours to observe for a localized cell-mediated reaction); Tuberculin skin test (PPD measurement).

Key Characteristics & Origin: Systemic autoimmune disease showing a strong female predominance (9:1); strongly associated with HLA-DR2 and HLA-DR3 alleles.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Mediates a Type III hypersensitivity reaction; autoantibodies bind to self-antigens (DNA/histones), forming immune complexes that deposit in small vessels and filters, activating complement and recruiting destructive neutrophils.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Malar 'butterfly' rash, discoid lupus, lupus nephritis (glomerulonephritis), arthritis, hematologic cytopenias, and neurological symptoms.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Positive ANA (sensitive screening); Anti-dsDNA and Anti-Smith autoantibodies (highly specific); decreased serum C3 and C4 complement levels.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Systemic inflammatory disease affecting joints; strong association with HLA-DR4. Characterized by the presence of Rheumatoid Factor (RF).
Primary Function & Mechanism: Mediates a mixed Type III/IV hypersensitivity. Autoreactive Th1 cells recruit macrophages that release destructive TNF-α in joint synovium. RF (IgM binding to IgG Fc tails) forms immune complexes that amplify inflammation.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Symmetrical polyarthritis (morning stiffness, joint erosions, pannus formation), subcutaneous nodules, systemic vasculitis, and pulmonary fibrosis.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Positive Rheumatoid Factor (RF); highly specific Anti-Cyclic Citrullinated Peptide (anti-CCP) antibodies; elevated ESR and CRP.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Type II (antibody-mediated) hypersensitivity; highly associated with HLA-DR3; often associated with thymic hyperplasia or thymoma.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Autoantibodies (IgG) bind to and block nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (AChR) at the neuromuscular junction, triggering receptor internalization, complement-mediated destruction, and impaired synaptic transmission.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Progressive muscle weakness and fatiguability (worse with exercise, improves with rest), ptosis, diplopia, dysphagia, and potentially fatal respiratory failure (myasthenic crisis).
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Anti-AChR antibodies (highly specific); Anti-Muscle-Specific Tyrosine Kinase (MuSK) antibodies; electromyography (EMG) decremental response.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Group of genetic disorders; most common is X-linked (IL2RG mutation). Autosomal recessive forms include adenosine deaminase (ADA) deficiency and RAG1/RAG2 mutations.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Severe defect in both cellular and humoral immunity. RAG1/RAG2 mutations block the V(D)J recombination needed to build functional B and T cell receptors, leaving lymphocytes totally non-functional.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Infants present with severe, recurrent infections (bacterial, viral, fungal, protozoal), chronic diarrhea, failure to thrive, and absence of thymic shadow. Fatal in infancy without bone marrow transplant.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Absent or extremely low T and B cell counts on flow cytometry; absence of T-cell receptor excision circles (TRECs) on newborn screening.

Key Characteristics & Origin: X-linked recessive immunodeficiency caused by a loss-of-function mutation in the Bruton's Tyrosine Kinase (BTK) gene on chromosome Xq22.
Primary Function & Mechanism: BTK is required for pre-B cell receptor signaling; its defect blocks pre-B cells from maturing into mature B cells in the bone marrow, causing a near-total absence of B cells and all immunoglobulin classes.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Male infants present after age 3-6 months (as maternal IgG wanes) with recurrent, severe pyogenic bacterial infections (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) of the respiratory tract.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Profound B-cell lymphopenia (<1% CD19+ B cells in peripheral blood) on flow cytometry; extremely low or undetectable levels of serum IgG, IgA, and IgM.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Congenital immunodeficiency caused by a microdeletion on chromosome 22q11.2, resulting in defective development of the 3rd and 4th pharyngeal pouches.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Causes thymic hypoplasia or aplasia, resulting in deficient T cell maturation and impaired cell-mediated immunity. Also causes parathyroid hypoplasia, leading to low calcium.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Recurrent viral, fungal, and opportunistic infections; cleft palate; congenital heart defects (conotruncal anomalies); tetany due to severe hypocalcemia.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Absent or profoundly low CD3+ T cell counts with normal B cell counts; absence of thymic shadow on chest X-ray; FISH/microarray showing 22q11.2 microdeletion.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Acquired clonal stem cell disorder caused by a somatic mutation in the PIGA gene, leading to a deficiency of GPI-anchor proteins.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Loss of GPI anchors causes a complete deficiency of cell-surface complement regulators DAF (CD55) and CD59 (MIRL), leaving red blood cells highly vulnerable to uncontrolled bystander complement-mediated MAC lysis.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Intravascular hemolytic anemia, hemoglobinuria (dark morning urine), severe thrombosis (especially in atypical venous sites), and pancytopenia.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry analysis showing absence of CD55 and CD59 on red blood cells and granulocytes.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Encoded by classical HLA-A, B, and C genes. Composed of an alpha heavy chain and a non-polymorphic beta-2 microglobulin chain. Distributed on all nucleated cells.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds and displays endogenous peptide antigens (viral or mutated intracellular proteins processed by proteasomes) to CD8+ Cytotoxic T cells.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Crucial for viral clearance and tumor surveillance; down-regulated by many viruses to escape detection; HLA-B27 strongly associated with Ankylosing Spondylitis.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry for surface MHC Class I/HLA expression; DNA-based molecular HLA typing.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Encoded by classical HLA-DP, DQ, and DR genes. Composed of an alpha and beta heterodimer. Expressed primarily on professional Antigen Presenting Cells (APCs).
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds and displays exogenous peptide antigens (extracellular pathogens processed via the endosomal-lysosomal pathway) to CD4+ Helper T cells.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Key mediator of CD4+ T helper cell activation and immune collaboration; HLA-DR4 associated with Rheumatoid Arthritis; HLA-DR3/DR4 associated with Type 1 Diabetes.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry for HLA-DP, DQ, DR; PCR-based HLA typing.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Originates in the bone marrow; resides as immature sentinel cells in peripheral tissues. The most potent 'professional' Antigen Presenting Cells (APCs).
Primary Function & Mechanism: Captures, processes, and displays exogenous antigens on MHC Class II (and Class I via cross-presentation). Matures and migrates to lymph nodes to express co-stimulatory molecules (B7) and activate naive T cells.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Acts as the essential bridge between innate and adaptive immunity; crucial for initiating primary adaptive immune responses and maintaining central/peripheral self-tolerance.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry identification using surface markers CD11c, HLA-DR, CD80, CD83, and CD86.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Derived from circulating blood monocytes; differentiates into tissue-specific residents (e.g., microglia, Kupffer cells, alveolar macrophages). Activated by IFN-γ or PAMPs.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Functions as professional phagocytes that engulf and digest pathogens/debris. Acts as APCs displaying antigens on MHC Class II to effector T cells at the site of inflammation; secretes pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α).
Clinical & Disease Associations: Primary cells involved in chronic inflammation, granuloma formation (e.g., in tuberculosis and leprosy), and the pathogenesis of septic shock (via excessive TNF-α release).
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Immunohistochemical staining or flow cytometry using markers CD14, CD68, CD11b, and HLA-DR.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Large granular lymphocytes originating from lymphoid progenitors but functioning as part of the innate immune system. No antigen-specific receptors.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Recognizes and destroys virus-infected and tumor cells. Employs the 'missing self' hypothesis to target cells lacking MHC Class I; also executes ADCC via Fc receptor CD16.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Involved in early defense against intracellular infections (especially herpesviruses) and cancers; defects lead to severe recurrent viral infections.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry markers CD3- and CD56+ / CD16+; functional NK cytotoxicity assays.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Development is promoted by IL-12 and IFN-γ; driven by the T-bet transcription factor.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Drives cell-mediated immunity against intracellular pathogens. Secretes IFN-γ to strongly activate macrophages, IL-2 to promote T cell proliferation, and TNF-β to mediate localized tissue inflammation.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Orchestrates Type IV Delayed-Type Hypersensitivity reactions (e.g., Tuberculin skin test, contact dermatitis); implicated in chronic inflammatory autoimmune diseases like Crohn's disease.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Intracellular cytokine staining for IFN-γ; CD4+ T cell flow cytometry panel; positive Tuberculin (PPD) skin test.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Differentiation is induced by IL-4; driven by the GATA3 transcription factor.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Promotes humoral (antibody-mediated) immunity and defense against extracellular parasites (helminths). Secretes IL-4 (induces IgE class switching), IL-5 (recruits/activates eosinophils), and IL-10 (suppresses Th1 responses).
Clinical & Disease Associations: Implicated in Type I hypersensitivity allergic reactions (asthma, eczema, anaphylaxis); genetic predisposition to atopy.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Intracellular cytokine staining for IL-4, IL-5, and IL-13; elevated serum IgE levels; peripheral blood eosinophilia.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Differentiated CD4+ T helper cell subset. Differentiation is promoted by IL-6, TGF-β, and IL-23; driven by the RORγt transcription factor.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Recruits neutrophils and maintains mucosal/epithelial barriers against extracellular bacteria and fungi by secreting IL-17 and IL-22.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Autosomal dominant Hyper-IgE syndrome (Job's syndrome) has Th17 deficiency; overactivity is associated with psoriasis, rheumatoid arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Intracellular cytokine staining for IL-17 via flow cytometry; serum IL-17 assay.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Subclass of CD4+ T cells characterized by the expression of CD25 and the Foxp3 transcription factor. Originates in thymus (nTregs) or peripheral tissues (iTregs).
Primary Function & Mechanism: Enforces peripheral self-tolerance by active suppression of self-reactive lymphocytes. Secretes anti-inflammatory cytokines IL-10 and TGF-β; utilizes CTLA-4 to downregulate co-stimulatory molecules on APCs.
Clinical & Disease Associations: IPEX syndrome (severe autoimmune disease marked by enteropathy, dermatological lesions, and polyendocrinopathy) is caused by Foxp3 mutation. Cancers recruit Tregs to escape immune destruction.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry showing CD4+ CD25+ Foxp3+; Foxp3 gene analysis.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Originates in the bone marrow and matures in the thymus (passing positive and negative selection). Recognizes peptide antigens presented on MHC Class I molecules.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Directly kills virus-infected, damaged, or tumor cells by inducing apoptosis. Employs the perforin/granzyme pathway (to form membrane pores and digest targets) and the Fas/FasL death receptor pathway.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Essential for viral clearance and tumor surveillance; implicated in transplant rejection (host-versus-graft disease) and Type IV cell-mediated hypersensitivity.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry identification using CD3+ and CD8+ surface markers; granzyme B and perforin enzyme-linked immunospot (ELISPOT) assays.

Key Characteristics & Origin: The most abundant complement protein in serum, produced mainly by the liver. Acts as the central convergence point for all three complement activation pathways.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Cleaved into C3a (anaphylatoxin that recruits mast cells/neutrophils) and C3b (binds covalently to pathogens to mediate opsonization, and forms C5 convertases to amplify the terminal pathway).
Clinical & Disease Associations: Congenital C3 deficiency leads to severe, recurrent pyogenic infections (e.g., S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae) and severe immune complex-mediated glomerulonephritis.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum C3 quantitative levels (using nephelometry or radial immunodiffusion); CH50 and AH50 hemolytic complement assays.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Liver-synthesized serum glycoprotein. Cleaved by C5 convertases (C4b2a3b in classical/lectin; C3b2Bb in alternative) to initiate the terminal complement cascade.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Cleaved into C5a (a highly potent anaphylatoxin and neutrophil chemoattractant) and C5b. C5b sequentially binds C6, C7, C8, and multiple C9 proteins to form the Membrane Attack Complex (MAC/C5b-9).
Clinical & Disease Associations: C5 deficiency or terminal MAC pathway defects (C5-C9) result in high susceptibility to recurrent, life-threatening Neisseria meningitidis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae infections.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum C5 quantitative levels; CH50 assay (decreased/absent with normal C3 and C4 indicates terminal pathway deficiency).

Key Characteristics & Origin: Produced primarily by activated CD4+ T helper (Th1) cells; acts as a crucial autocrine and paracrine T cell growth factor.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds to high-affinity IL-2 receptors (containing CD25) to trigger clonal expansion, proliferation, and survival of T cells, B cells, NK cells, and regulatory T cells (Tregs).
Clinical & Disease Associations: Recombinant IL-2 (Aldesleukin) is used to treat metastatic renal cell carcinoma and melanoma; targeted by immunosuppressive drugs like Cyclosporine and Tacrolimus.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum cytokine assays; expression of CD25 (alpha chain of IL-2R) on the surface of T lymphocytes by flow cytometry.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Secreted by CD4+ Th2 cells, mast cells, and activated basophils. Classic pleiotropic cytokine.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Induces differentiation of naive CD4+ T cells into the Th2 helper phenotype. Directs B cell class-switching to IgE and IgG4, and promotes eosinophil tissue recruitment.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Key driver of atopic allergic reactions (allergic rhinitis, asthma, atopic dermatitis); targeted by Dupilumab (anti-IL-4Rα).
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum IL-4 level by ELISA; intracellular cytokine staining on T cells.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Type II interferon; homodimeric glycoprotein produced mainly by activated CD4+ Th1 cells, CD8+ CTLs, and Natural Killer (NK) cells.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds to Type II IFN receptors to activate the JAK-STAT pathway. Acts as the primary battle cytokine that activates macrophages, enhances MHC Class I and II expression on APCs, and blocks IL-4-induced IgE switching.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Recombinant IFN-γ (Actimmune) is used to treat Chronic Granulomatous Disease (CGD) by boosting macrophage bactericidal activity; crucial for tuberculosis clearance.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: IFN-γ release assays (IGRA) for tuberculosis screening (e.g., QuantiFERON-TB Gold); intracellular cytokine flow cytometry.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Homotrimeric cytokine produced mainly by activated macrophages, T cells, and NK cells in response to PAMP/DAMP recognition.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Coordinates local and systemic inflammation. Induces vascular endothelium adhesion molecules, increases vascular permeability, recruits neutrophils, and triggers hepatocytes to release acute-phase proteins.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Central mediator of rheumatoid arthritis joint destruction, Crohn's disease inflammation, and septic shock; triggers cachexia (wasting syndrome) in chronic infections and malignancy.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serum TNF-α concentration; acute-phase reactants (CRP and ESR) as surrogates.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Family of calcium-dependent carbohydrate-binding transmembrane proteins. L-selectin on leukocytes; E- and P-selectin on activated endothelial cells.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Interacts with mucin-like ligands (CD15s) to mediate the initial weak, transient 'rolling' phase of leukocyte extravasation along vessel walls.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Deficient selectin ligand expression causes Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 2 (LAD II), presenting with severe immune deficiencies, high leukocytosis, and developmental delay.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry evaluating CD15s (sialyl Lewis X) expression on neutrophils; genetic testing for SLC35C1 mutations.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Heterodimeric cell-surface glycoproteins composed of non-covalently associated alpha and beta subunits. Examples include LFA-1 (CD11a/CD18) and Mac-1.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds tightly to immunoglobulin-superfamily ligands (like ICAM-1) on endothelial cells, converting leukocyte 'rolling' into stable 'tight adhesion' during extravasation.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Loss-of-function mutation in the common beta-2 integrin chain CD18 gene causes Leukocyte Adhesion Deficiency Type 1 (LAD I), marked by recurrent infections without pus, delayed umbilical cord separation.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Flow cytometry confirming complete or partial absence of surface CD18/CD11b on peripheral blood granulocytes.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Small, non-proteinaceous chemical compound of low molecular weight (e.g., penicillin, urushiol in poison ivy). It is reactive but non-immunogenic on its own.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds covalently to a high-molecular-weight host carrier protein, creating a hapten-carrier complex that is recognized as foreign, stimulating antibody and T-cell responses.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Drug-induced autoimmune hemolytic anemia (Type II hypersensitivity); urushiol contact dermatitis (Type IV hypersensitivity).
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Clinical diagnosis; allergen patch testing; specific IgE or drug-induced antibody screening.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Bacterial or viral proteins (e.g., S. aureus TSST-1, S. pyogenes exotoxins) that bypass normal MHC presentation rules.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Binds directly and simultaneously to the outer face of MHC Class II molecules on APCs and the Vβ domain of T-cell receptors (TCRs), cross-linking them without processing. Activates up to 20% of all T cells.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Triggers Toxic Shock Syndrome (TSS) and food poisoning, inducing a catastrophic 'cytokine storm' (massive release of TNF-α, IL-1, IFN-γ) leading to severe fever, hypotension, and shock.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Bacterial cultures from infection sites; TSST-1 toxin detection via PCR or immunological assays; multi-organ failure screening (CMP, lactate).

Key Characteristics & Origin: Enzyme-Linked Immunosorbent Assay. A highly sensitive, solid-phase in vitro serological diagnostic method using microtiter plates.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Combines antibody-antigen binding specificity with enzyme-catalyzed substrate reactions (e.g., using horseradish peroxidase) to produce a quantifiable color change.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Standard screening method for HIV antibodies, food allergies (specific IgE), autoimmune disease autoantibodies (e.g., anti-dsDNA), and circulating cytokines.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Spectrophotometric reading of optical density (OD) to quantify target concentrations.

Key Characteristics & Origin: Vaccines made from weakened (attenuated) live pathogens that maintain their replication capacity but lose their pathogenicity.
Primary Function & Mechanism: Replicates transiently inside host cells, delivering vaccine antigens to both MHC Class I and Class II pathways, generating highly durable humoral and cellular (memory CD8+ CTL) immunity.
Clinical & Disease Associations: Examples: Measles, Mumps, Rubella (MMR), Varicella, Oral Polio (Sabin). Contraindicated in pregnant women and immunocompromised individuals due to safety/reversion risks.
Diagnostic Markers / Lab Tests: Serological antibody titer screening (post-vaccination IgG levels) confirming immunity.
